name: PT Pelat Timah Nusantara Tbk

frontmatter.title: Latinusa: the sole Indonesian tinplate maker, priced for a recovery its cash flow does not fund
frontmatter.summary: Latinusa is Indonesia's only tinplate producer, a converter that buys imported steel substrate and tin and sells coated coil and sheet to food, beverage and battery canners. The profit recovery is real, but working capital absorbs roughly half of every incremental dollar of sales, EBIT margins are thin and net debt is several times EBITDA. At Rp140 the shares discount a recovery the DCF does not support.
thesis: Sole domestic producer with a real franchise: the only tinplate roller in Indonesia, capacity raised to an installed base lifted by the 2025 revamp, and newly qualified as a supplier to a multinational ready-to-drink brand that previously imported all of its can stock.

The FY2026 recovery is genuine but small: nine-month revenue rose by a fifth and net profit turned positive, yet the company guides to a low single-digit net margin and the gross margin sits inside the five-year range, below the 2022 packaging-boom peak.

Working capital, not the plant, is the binding constraint: receivables run at roughly five months of sales against two weeks of payables, so growth is funded by debt and the incremental return on that capital sits below our cost of capital.

Cash flow does not cover the current price: even at the top of the historical margin range and with the tin price normalising, our DCF lands well below the market, and the target comes from the discounted cash flow rather than from the boom-era multiples the stock once traded on.

Downside is floored by assets: Cilegon and Sidoarjo land is carried at an independent appraisal and book equity is a multiple of the market capitalisation, which is why we call the shares an avoid rather than a short in a stock with a free float under a sixth of the capital.

blocks.text: **SELL — target Rp18, -83.4% against the Rp140 price** (the total-return figure includes the next twelve months' dividend of Rp5). Latinusa is a single-product converter: it imports black plate and tin, rolls and coats them into tinplate coil and sheet, and sells to Indonesian can makers serving food, beverage, battery and chemical end markets [S2]. It is the only such plant in the country and has installed capacity of 160,000 t a year [S2]. On the operating side the story has improved: nine-month revenue to September 2026 was 117 USD m and net profit 1.5 USD m, against a small loss a year earlier, and management guides to revenue of about 160 USD m and net profit of 3.0 USD m for the full year [S3][S4].

We are not disputing the recovery. We are disputing the price. The company earns a gross margin in the mid single digits and an EBIT margin that has averaged one to two per cent over five years, because the steel substrate and the tin are globally priced inputs it cannot control and the canners it sells to are large, concentrated customers [S2]. Layered on top is a balance sheet that turns those thin margins into a levered equity stub: net debt of USD53.5m against EBITDA of USD8.5m in our base year, with interest taking a large slice of operating profit before tax [S2][S3].

Our base case is the most probable path, not a cautious one. We carry the company's own volume plan, a gross margin of 6.7% this year drifting to 7.0% — inside the five-year range, above the FY2025A 5.8% but still below the FY2022A packaging-boom peak of 7.7% — SG&A net of the recurring scrap credit that the LK carries inside operating profit [S2], and revenue growth of 15.8% followed by a mid single-digit path [S2][S3][S4]. On those assumptions the discounted cash flow is worth Rp0 per share before the twelve-month roll-forward — a floored zero, because the unfloored equity value is negative against the debt — and the weighted target after the liquidity discount is Rp18. The gap to the market is not driven by a punitive discount rate — our WACC of 9.8% sits inside the house band for a dollar-reporting industrial — but by cash conversion: working capital is 53.0% of revenue, so each extra dollar of sales ties up about half a dollar of cash, and the return on that incremental capital is below the cost of it [S2].

What would make us wrong is a durable step-up in margin, not a cyclical one. The bull case is worth Rp136 because tighter import enforcement, a richer premium and ready-to-drink mix and a normalising tin price could lift the margin enough to change the arithmetic; the bear case floors at Rp0 because the equity is thin enough to be wiped out by a margin give-back [S4][S2]. We attach 60% to base, 25% to bear and 15% to bull, giving a probability-weighted target of Rp20 before the liquidity discount.

Two things keep this from being a short. First, the asset base: land in Cilegon and Sidoarjo is carried at an independent appraisal and book equity is a multiple of the market capitalisation, so a rational controller has options a cash-flow model does not capture [S2]. Second, the register: a Japanese steel consortium holds the large majority, the free float is well under a fifth of the shares and daily traded value is thin, so the price can stay detached from value for longer than a short can survive [S0][S2]. We rate the shares an avoid and would revisit on evidence of structural margin change, not on a lower share price alone.

Latinusa — PT Pelat Timah Nusantara Tbk — has operated for more than three decades as Indonesia's tinplate producer, and the annual report states plainly that it remains the sole domestic manufacturer of tinplate packaging for food, beverage, battery and chemical applications [S2]. Manufacturing sits in the Krakatau industrial estate at Cilegon, Banten, with marketing and sales run from Jakarta; the company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2009 under the ticker NIKL [S2]. The plant runs on world-scale tinplate technology with food-safety and green-industry certification, which matters in a business where the customer is a branded food or beverage company auditing its packaging supply chain [S2].

The product split is two lines, not two businesses. Coil is the large majority of sales and sheet the rest, with coil carrying the thinner margin and sheet the better one after the coating and cutting steps [S2]. The distinction matters for mix: the stated strategy is to push the share of premium and ready-to-drink customers, where specifications are tighter and the price per tonne is better, and the company reports that the milk segment rose from a quarter to slightly more of sales in the latest year while dry food fell as consumers moved away from large canned formats [S4].

The customer base is the Indonesian canning industry, so the demand driver is household consumption of canned milk, processed food, soft drinks and, increasingly, batteries and industrial packaging [S2]. That is a mature, import-competed end market. Management puts national tinplate demand at around 200,000 t, below the 250,000 t peak of 2022, and notes that domestic installed capacity is below national consumption, so imports — chiefly from China and Korea — fill the gap [S4][S2]. Latinusa's answer is to defend domestic share against imports and to compete on quality and service for premium segments rather than on price for commodity can stock [S2].

The raw-material chain is the most important thing to understand about the model. The steel substrate is imported, and tin metal is bought domestically from PT Timah under a contract priced off the London Metal Exchange average plus a fixed premium of US$340/t per tonne; the 2026 contract covers 595 t, down from 685 t in 2025 and 790 t in 2024 [S3][S2]. The contracted tonnage is the volume under the PT Timah supply agreement, not necessarily the whole tin requirement — the agreement runs to 31 December 2026 and the balance of consumption is bought spot at the same LME reference — so a lower contracted volume is consistent with a year of higher production on thinner coatings, and it is not a statement about output [S3]. The key point is the currency. Both inputs are dollar-priced while output is sold in rupiah: every dollar of trade receivables is rupiah-denominated (62.0 USD m) [S3], so a weaker rupiah cuts the dollar value of sales without touching the dollar cost of substrate and tin, and the P&L is exposed at the gross-margin line, not just below it. On top of that, 45.6 USD m of the short-term bank loans are rupiah liabilities, which is where the translation losses in the net-income line come from — the nine-month 2026 net currency loss was 0.8 USD m [S3]. Management's own summary is that all raw materials are imported while sales must be in rupiah [S4].

Ownership is concentrated and strategic. The controlling block is a Japanese consortium holding fifty-five per cent — Nippon Steel Corporation, Mitsui & Co., Nippon Steel Trading Corporation and Metal One — with Nippon Steel the largest single holder; PT Krakatau Steel remains a shareholder and a service provider from the adjacent estate [S2]. That is both an asset and a governance question: it gives the company access to the global steel network and to Nippon Steel's technical support, and it means a material share of raw-material purchasing runs through a related party, which we treat in the governance section [S2]. The register leaves a free float of about a seventh of the shares and a small daily traded value, which shapes how the stock trades [S0].

The competitive position is a protected niche with a weak moat. Latinusa is the only domestic producer, it holds certifications and customer qualifications a new entrant would need years to obtain, and its site inside a steel estate gives logistics and utility advantages [S2]. But a sole domestic producer with a large share of the market supplied by imports has no pricing power: the import parity price sets the ceiling, the globally priced substrate sets the floor, and the margin is the difference between them less conversion cost [S2][S4]. Those are a converter's economics, which is why we model a margin business rather than a commodity producer with reserves and a royalty.

The Indonesian tinplate market is small, mature and structurally short of domestic capacity. Management sizes national demand at about 200,000 t against the 250,000 t peak of 2022 and describes installed domestic capacity as insufficient to meet consumption, with the balance imported [S4][S2]. That combination — a market that has shrunk from its peak but still imports a large share of its needs — defines the competitive problem. Imports from China and Korea are priced aggressively because the global steel system is in oversupply, and the annual report cites the OECD's estimate of planned steelmaking capacity expansion through 2027 against world demand growth of well under one per cent a year, with most of the new capacity in Asia [S2]. A domestic roller competing against that price set has to run at high utilisation on a fixed cost base simply to hold its margin.

The demand side is the Indonesian consumer. Tinplate goes into canned milk, processed food, beverages, batteries and chemical packaging, so the drivers are household consumption, the mix between large canned formats and ready-to-drink packs, and the substitution battle against plastic and aluminium [S2][S4]. Management argues that the Middle East conflict, by raising plastic and international freight costs, has made tinplate more competitive as a substitute and imports less attractive — a rare case of a geopolitical shock helping a domestic converter [S4]. We treat that as a real but temporary tailwind rather than a structural change in the competitive balance.

Regulation cuts both ways. The company's own account of its strategy is that it lobbies for stricter surveillance of imports it regards as unfairly priced, while its cost base is dominated by imported raw materials, so any broad restriction raises its own input costs [S4][S5]. Trade remedies and standards on finished tinplate, rather than on substrate alone, are the swing factor: the competitive position improves if enforcement tightens on finished coil and sheet and worsens if substrate becomes harder or dearer to import.

On the five-forces view the picture is unfavourable on three axes. Supplier power is high: substrate is a globally traded steel product sourced from a small number of mills, and part of the purchasing runs through the controlling shareholder's trading arm [S2]. Buyer power is high: customers are large branded food and beverage companies that qualify suppliers, set specifications and can switch or import [S2][S4]. The threat of substitutes is real, from plastic and aluminium packaging, and it moves with relative packaging costs [S4]. The threat of new entrants is low, which is the one favourable axis, because a greenfield tinplate line needs capital, customer qualification and permits the incumbent already holds [S2]. Rivalry is moderate but import-mediated: the incumbent does not fight a domestic peer, it fights the import parity price.

The moat, in other words, is a licence-and-qualification moat, not a pricing moat. That has two consequences for valuation. It justifies a long forecast horizon, because the plant will not be displaced by a domestic competitor. It does not justify a margin above the historical range, because the import parity price caps it. The annual report's own account of 2025 supports that reading: sales realisation reached ninety-one per cent of the target set at the start of the year and production ninety per cent of its target, with the shortfall attributed to import competition and the global price decline [S2].

Demand recovery is the base case but not a strong one. Management plans production up by about a tenth and sales volume up by a similar amount in 2026, and the nine-month numbers show revenue up by a fifth, consistent with volume recovery plus better mix [S2][S3]. We carry that recovery and then let growth settle to a mid single-digit rate, because the end market is mature and the company's share among domestic producers is already dominant. We do not assume it wins share from imports beyond the recovery already visible in the order book.

The five-year record is a cycle, not a trend. Revenue fell from USD255.3m in FY2022, the post-pandemic packaging boom, to USD171.1m, USD155.7m and USD139.8m as selling prices followed global tinplate prices down and volumes softened [S2]. Gross profit collapsed from USD19.6m to USD1.6m before recovering to USD9.4m and USD8.1m, and EBIT went from USD14.3m to a loss of USD-4.0m and back to USD4.6m and USD3.8m [S2]. The swing between the best and worst year is the most important fact about this equity: a converter with a fixed cost base and no pricing power turns a small change in spread into a very large change in profit.

Our forecast starts from the 2026 actuals rather than the FY2025 trough. Nine-month revenue of 117 USD m is already well ahead of the comparable period, nine-month gross profit of 7.8 USD m is well above the 5.1 USD m of the same nine months a year earlier although still short of the whole of FY2025 (USD8.1m), and net profit was 1.5 USD m [S3]. Management's full-year targets are revenue of about 160 USD m and net profit 3.0 USD m [S4]. We model FY2026E revenue of USD161.9m, EBITDA of USD8.5m and net profit of USD2.3m: revenue holds the fourth quarter at the prior-year fourth quarter and so lands near the revenue target, but profit does not reach the net-profit guidance, because at the observed nine-month gross margin and the restated fixed-cost base the profit target needs a gross margin above anything the company has printed in five years [S2][S3]. From there revenue grows 4.0% and then at a similar rate, reaching USD188.5m by the end of the forecast, with volume recovering toward the national demand level the company cites and prices flat in nominal dollars [S4].

Margins are the second assumption and the one that carries the valuation. We model a gross margin of 6.7% in FY2026E, which is the nine-month actual, rising to 7.0% as premium and ready-to-drink mix improves and the tin price normalises from the 2026 squeeze toward the desk's through-cycle anchor [S3][S2]. That is not a cautious number: the best gross margin of the last five years was set in the 2022 boom at 7.7%, and we hold the terminal margin inside the observed range — below that peak and above the 5.8% FY2025A trough — rather than at either extreme [S2]. Operating costs are held at 2.9% of sales this year, the nine-month run rate, and drift to 2.6% because management is holding the dollar cost base flat while revenue grows [S3][S4]. The resulting EBIT margin is 3.8% this year and 4.4% by FY2028E.

The cost line deserves separate attention because it is where tin bites. Raw-material usage was 114 USD m of a 132 USD m cost of goods sold in FY2025, so substrate and tin are the overwhelming majority of cost and everything else — salaries, energy, packaging, maintenance, depreciation — is a small tail [S2]. Tin is the smaller part of that: contracted purchases of 685 t in 2025 at LME-linked prices imply a bill in the low tens of millions of dollars, a meaningful but not dominant share of cost [S2]. The 2026 tin price has been volatile enough to matter, and the nine-month gross margin rising despite it is the best evidence that the input is largely passed through with a lag rather than absorbed [S3].

Depreciation is where the data pack misleads. The reported D&A in the source data is a fraction of the real charge: the fixed-asset note shows total property depreciation of 1.8 USD m in FY2025 plus right-of-use depreciation, against a figure roughly eight times smaller in the pack [S2]. We restate the last two fiscal years from the notes, which lifts historical EBITDA to the level shown in the table above and changes the starting point for every multiple in the valuation section [S2]. The correction matters because a capital-intensive converter carrying USD22.7m of net fixed assets cannot depreciate them at a rate implying a useful life measured in centuries; the restated charge is consistent with the asset base and with the capex actually spent [S2].

Cash flow is the crux, and it is where the recovery story weakens. Free cash flow to the firm was USD8.0m in FY2025 against net profit of USD1.0m, so earnings were converted into cash comfortably [S2]. But the level of working capital is extraordinary. Operating working capital was USD77.4m in FY2025, more than half of that year's revenue, and a similar share in FY2024; the 30 September 2026 balance sheet is heavier still — receivables of 62.0 USD m against bank loans of 58.9 USD m [S3]. We carry 53.0% of revenue, the two-year average, in every forecast year [S2][S3]. Receivables run at roughly five months of sales and payables at about a month — the signature of a supplier with weak bargaining power buying imported substrate on cash terms and selling to large domestic customers on extended rupiah terms. That structure, not the profit and loss account, is what makes the balance sheet fragile: a tenth of the receivables book is worth more than a year of net profit. Free cash flow to the firm was negative in the 2022 boom year because the working capital build swallowed the earnings, and it was negative at the interims of 2026 for the same reason [S2][S3].

That is why growth is double-edged here. In our base case revenue growth of around 4.0% requires an increase in working capital of USD3.4m at a 53.0% ratio, against capex of USD2.2m and cash tax of USD1.0m, out of EBITDA of USD9.5m [S2]. At that ratio the company keeps almost none of its operating cash generation to service debt and pay dividends: every incremental dollar of revenue costs about half a dollar of working capital to earn a couple of cents of after-tax operating profit, an incremental return far below the cost of capital. The 2026 half-year did not release working capital — the 30 September LK shows receivables and inventories higher than at the year-end and the short-term bank loans up to fund them — so our forecast has debt rising with working capital rather than falling [S3].

The balance sheet is the second constraint. At the last audited year-end the company carried cash of USD7.1m and debt of USD54.3m against equity of USD56.9m, so net debt was USD47.3m and net debt to EBITDA on our FY2026E number is 6.3x [S2]. Interest expense of USD2.6m absorbs a large share of EBIT of USD6.2m, the definition of a levered equity stub [S3]. Debt has not fallen: it was reduced into 2025 but the 2026 working-capital build lifted short-term bank loans to 58.9 USD m at 30 September, and we carry that in the valuation as net debt of 58.9 USD m less cash of 8.5 USD m, not the June figure [S3]. Our forecast therefore has net borrowing of USD4.9m in FY2026E and continued small increases while revenue grows at a working-capital ratio near 53.0%, with a first repayment only at the end of the horizon [S3]. That is what keeps net debt to EBITDA near 6.3x and the interest burden near half of EBIT; if the working-capital ratio falls, both improve sharply.

Capital allocation is conservative to the point of inertia. Capex was USD0.8m in FY2025, below the restated depreciation charge, after the revamp and boiler work of the prior years [S2]. The dividend policy targets a stated range of net profit, and the FY2025 dividend paid in April 2026 sat at the bottom of that range — consistent with a board keeping cash for working capital and debt service [S2]. There has been no rights issue, buyback or acquisition, and the share count has not changed since listing [S2]. We model a payout of 30.0%, the observed floor of the policy.

Earnings quality is mixed but not alarming. Cash conversion is good: cumulative operating cash flow over the last three years comfortably exceeds cumulative net profit, the accruals ratio is negative, and there is no sign of revenue booked ahead of cash [S2]. The flags are structural rather than accounting. Receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025 even as both fell, the classic warning of collection stretch [S2]. A material share of raw-material purchases runs through the controlling shareholder's trading arm — 29.3 USD m in FY2025, about a fifth of cost of goods sold [S2]. The auditor is a mid-tier firm rather than a Big Four practice [S2]. And the share price itself has looked manipulated: a limit-up run in late 2025 followed by a fall of roughly two thirds through 2026 on a float of about a seventh of the capital, a flow story rather than an accounting one but worth stating plainly [S0].

We value Latinusa on a discounted free cash flow to the firm, with the operating asset value cross-checked against book and against a reverse DCF of the current price. The method choice follows the business, not a house habit. Latinusa is not a compounder with a reinvestment runway: it owns one plant, sells a largely undifferentiated commodity into an import-competed market, and its capacity is already installed [S2]. It is not a commodity producer either — there is no reserve, no benchmark price it sets, no royalty and no grade. What it is, is a capital-intensive converter whose equity value is the present value of the spread between tinplate prices and substrate costs, minus the working capital that spread consumes. A cash flow model with an explicit terminal value is the only construction that captures all three of those, and it is the reason we drop the P/E weight the industry default would carry: at a net profit of USD2.3m, one contract negotiation moves earnings per share by more than any multiple does [S2]. Book value is kept as a cross-check rather than a method, because the plant is real and insured but it is also a single-purpose asset with no alternative use.

The cost of capital is where the valuation starts to bite. The house build begins with a US dollar risk-free rate of 4.9%, adds an equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesian country risk premium of 2.5%, and applies an unlevered beta of 0.80 — the industry default for a cyclical materials converter, which is right here because both the substrate and the end market are cyclical [S2]. Gearing does the rest. With net debt at 2.00 times market capitalisation, a cap the model applies because the shares have fallen so far that the market weight of equity no longer reflects the economics of the capital structure, the levered beta is 2.05 and the cost of equity is 18.6%. That 2.00 times is the model's cap, not the market's own ratio: the equity trades far below book value, so the market's own debt-to-equity is above the cap and the relevered beta we use is the less punitive of the two [S3][S0]. Debt costs 6.9% pre-tax in the WACC, which is the forward marginal rate (risk-free plus the corporate spread), while the P&L carries the legacy contracted rate of 4.7% that the filings actually show; the two are disclosed rather than smoothed, and the WACC rate is the right one for new debt raised to fund working capital. Tax in the WACC is the 22.0% statutory rate, while the P&L uses 25.0% because the filings show non-deductible items [S2][S3]. With equity at 33.3% of the capital structure the weighted average cost of capital is 9.8%. The valuation template is the industry default corporate set, and the DCF carries 100.0% of the weight: the multiples are disclosed in the cross-check table but not weighted, because at this profit level a single tin contract moves EPS more than any peer multiple, and there is no listed Indonesian tinplate peer to anchor one [S2][S0]. Justified P/B is not weighted either, and the reader should know why: at the 1.7% return the last audited year delivered against a 18.6% cost of equity, the Gordon-consistent P/B is a small fraction of book, so a second method would move the number by rounding and would put a second floored branch beside the first [S2][S3]. What that leaves is one honest output: the base case floored at Rp0 because the unfloored equity value is negative — enterprise value of USD34.4m against bank loans of 58.9 USD m less cash of 8.5 USD m at the valuation date, before the 0.2 USD m current and 0.2 USD m non-current lease liabilities and with the 7.2 USD m tax claim as the bridge, so the floor is hiding a negative number rather than a small one — and the target is the probability-weighted scenario value, not the base branch alone [S3][S0].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of USD34.4m and an equity value per share of Rp0, of which 81.0% sits in the terminal value. That terminal share is high for a business we have just called mature, and it is the honest number rather than a red flag: the explicit forecast has almost no free cash flow in it, because growth consumes working capital faster than the operating margin generates it. The value is in what the existing plant can earn once the company stops growing into its balance sheet, not in the growth we forecast. It is also why a model of this name is knife-edged: change the working capital ratio by a percentage point of sales and the answer moves by roughly a tenth. The terminal value is 81.0% of the enterprise value and is struck on FY2030E EBITDA of USD11.0m, which is an exit multiple far below the forward 8.6x times the stock trades on and below the 11.8x times of the last actual year [S0]. That is deliberate and it is the test the house card demands: the terminal cash flow is struck after a full working-capital charge and after capex, so it is not comparable with an EBITDA multiple on an unlevered, pre-reinvestment company — at a mid-cycle exit multiple the terminal value alone would add several tens of rupiah per share, and at five times FY2030E EBITDA the whole equity would be worth more than the DCF shows. We do not take that exit because the reinvestment that produces the EBITDA is exactly what consumes the cash.

What the assets are worth, and why that does not floor the target. Book equity is 58.1 USD m at 30 September 2026, of which 11.6 USD m is a fixed-asset revaluation surplus, so pre-revaluation book equity is materially lower [S3]; the register holds a controlling strategic block (Nippon Steel, Mitsui, Nippon Steel Trading, Metal One), Krakatau Steel and ASABRI, and the plant is the only tinplate line in the country at 160,000 t tonnes of capacity [S2]. On a liquidation arithmetic — receivables at face, inventory at cost, minus the bank loans — the assets would cover the whole market capitalisation. We do not use that as a target, and the reason is not conservatism: the receivables are five months old and only realisable at face if the customers pay, the plant has no alternative use, the controlling holder has announced no sale process and the free float is too small for a control transaction to clear without their agreement, and the company is a going concern whose rupiah funding is rolled by state-linked banks [S2][S3]. So the asset value is a floor on what somebody might pay in a control event, not a value an outside shareholder can realise inside twelve months. It is the reason the rating is SELL rather than a short: we are not paid for the gap between price and value with this float, and the gap can close upwards if a strategic buyer ever appears.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is instructive. On book value the shares are worth a third of what the balance sheet says — the market is not disputing the assets, it is disputing the return on them. Return on equity was 1.7% in the last audited year [S2], so a share trading at 0.3x times book is paying a price for a return well below the cost of equity; the discount is what the arithmetic says, not an anomaly. On own-history multiples the picture reverses: at 8.6x times forward EBITDA the stock looks cheap against its own boom-era average, and a mean-reversion screen would call it a buy [S0]. We do not use those means as targets. The boom-era multiples were set on a company earning a spread that no longer exists, on a float so thin that a single buyer could move the price, and applying them would be exactly the multiple-survival error the house card warns about: a high multiple earned in a peak year is a statement about the peak, not about the business. The same logic applies to the P/E of 8.7x times, which capitalises a profit level that a single tin contract can move.

The sensitivity grid is the most important table in this report, because it shows both what the value is and what it is not. It runs revenue growth against gross margin, not the working-capital and capex axes described here, and it has one dominant feature: most of its cells are floored, because the base equity value is negative before the floor and stays negative until the margin is lifted well above the base. On the margin axis alone, one point above our base at base growth is worth about half today's price after the liquidity discount, not nothing; two points above the base on our growth path does clear the price. On the growth axis, a path two points slower is worth more than our base at the base margin and above, because growth at these spreads consumes more working capital than it earns; the maximum in the grid pairs two points of extra margin with four points of slower growth, and the four-points-slower row at the base margin is itself above the share price and close to the growth rate the market is implying in the paragraph below. The honest shape of this equity is that the value is bought with margin, not with volume, and the margin has to come from somewhere a converter does not control. With working capital at 53.0% of sales, each extra point of growth needs about half a point of new capital to earn roughly two cents of after-tax operating profit, so growth at these spreads is worth less than standing still — the DCF's terminal value is built on a cash flow after a working-capital charge that eats most of the operating margin, and the model is not wrong to say so [S2][S3]. We keep the company's own growth plan as the base because that is what management is actually doing — FY2026 production 12.0% higher, sales 11.0% higher, and demand recovering toward 200,000 t — not because it is value-maximising; a board that stopped investing would be worth more per share, and that is a scenario, not a forecast [S2][S4]. The WACC and terminal-growth grid carries no information and we say so rather than dress it up: nearly every cell is floored at zero, because the base equity value is already negative and no discount rate in a one-point band fixes that — the single cell that escapes the floor is the one that pairs a lower WACC with a higher terminal growth, and it is worth a small fraction of the price. The discount-rate debate is not where this equity is decided. We apply a liquidity discount of 10.0% to the fundamental value for the free float and a daily traded value below the house investability threshold, and the resulting target is Rp18 against a price of Rp140, a total return of -83.4%. That is a SELL.

What does the price imply? At Rp140 the reverse DCF solves to FY2027E revenue growth of 0.76%, which is -3.2% away from the 4.0% we carry — a top line that stops growing, not one that compounds. That is the same answer the grid gives in the other direction: because a slower growth path is worth more at these spreads, the market is paying for the growth rate that destroys the least value, and the cell four points below our base at the base margin is worth more than the share price while our own path is worth nothing after the liquidity discount [S3][S0]. Read together, price and model agree on the arithmetic and disagree on the output, and the reason is that the market is pricing a business that stops reinvesting in working capital while we model the company's stated plan. The company is not wrong to expect the 2026 recovery; the nine-month results show it happening [S3]. What the price cannot be justified on is the recovery plus growth: the recovery arrives with a working-capital bill attached and a debt load that eats most of it, so the value has to come from margin — the grid says two points of it — and nothing in the filings shows a converter holding two points of additional spread through a tin cycle [S2].

The risk table is short but unusually loaded, because this is a small, geared, illiquid company in a commodity with a political price. We score each risk by likelihood over the next two years and by the damage it does to the value in the valuation section.

**Regulatory and trade policy — high likelihood, high impact.** The company's entire competitive position rests on trade remedies against imported tinplate and on the food-contact standards that make its plant qualify as a supplier [S2][S4]. A loosening of either, or a trade agreement that admits Chinese or Korean coil at landed prices below domestic cost, compresses the spread to zero and takes the equity with it. The asymmetry is brutal: the stock is priced as if protection is permanent.

**Tin and substrate cost — high likelihood, medium impact.** Tin purchases are contracted at LME-linked prices and the 2026 spike is already visible in the nine-month cost line [S3][S2]. The pass-through is partial and lagged, so a sustained tin price at the top of its range for two quarters is enough to erase the forecast margin. The mitigating factor is that a converter with an order book can re-price; the aggravating factor is that the company's largest customers are food canners with their own pricing power.

**Volume and demand — medium likelihood, high impact.** National tinplate demand sits around 200,000 t against a 2022 peak of 250,000 t [S4], and FY2025 sales realised only 91.0% of target [S2]. The company plans sales volume growth of 11.0% for 2026 [S2]. If the recovery in demand is a restocking cycle rather than a new level, the volume line falls back and the operating leverage works against us — the FY2023 loss of USD-4.0m is the template [S2].

**Currency and interest — high likelihood, high impact.** The exposure is inverted relative to a dollar exporter: revenue is rupiah (every dollar of trade receivables is rupiah-denominated) while the steel substrate and tin are imported in dollars, so a rupiah depreciation cuts the dollar revenue line without touching the dollar cost of inputs [S3][S4]. The liability side is rupiah too — 45.6 USD m of the short-term bank loans — so a weaker rupiah produces translation losses on the debt as well, and the nine-month 2026 net currency loss of 0.8 USD m is the channel in action [S3]. The macro backdrop the desk carries — balance-of-payments pressure and a cautious stance on the rupiah — makes this a live risk rather than a tail [S3].

**Governance and related parties — medium likelihood, high impact.** A fifth of raw-material purchases run through the controlling shareholder's trading arm [S2], which means the transfer price of the company's largest cost line is set by the party that controls it. That is disclosed, audited and not by itself improper, but it caps what a minority holder can be sure of. Weak liquidity compounds it: with a free float of about a seventh of the capital and daily turnover of a few billion rupiah, an institution cannot exit on the numbers.

**Liquidity and flow — high likelihood, high impact on price.** The price history of the last year is a limit-up run followed by a two-thirds fall on a thin float [S0]. That is a flow regime, not a valuation regime, and it is the reason our target carries a liquidity discount.

Our bear case assumes imports win, tin rises a fifth with only half the cost recovered in price, the rupiah slips further against the dollar and volume growth stalls: revenue growth gives back a point, the gross margin gives back two points (the tin channel plus the currency channel) and the net FX line worsens, so the equity floors at its limited-liability value and no more. Our bull case mirrors all three shocks exactly in the opposite direction — trade enforcement holds, the premium and ready-to-drink contracts lift mix as management plans, tin eases toward the desk's through-cycle anchor and the rupiah firms — so margin holds at the top of its range [S2][S4]. The scenario values are Rp0 to Rp136, and the tails are not symmetric in the model: the bear lands on the limited-liability floor of zero because bank loans of 58.9 USD m less cash of 8.5 USD m swamp the operating value at a lower margin, while the bull re-rates the equity. We put 60% on the base because it is the most probable path, 25% on the bear, and only 15% on the bull: the bull needs the gross margin two points above the base, above the 7.7% FY2022A peak and above anything in the filings, so it is a low-probability tail rather than a coin-flip. On these probabilities the modal outcome is zero — the base branch is floored at Rp0 — so the published probability-weighted value of Rp20 is an option on the bull branch, not a central cash-flow value. The reader should see that construction plainly: this stock is a call option on the spread, not a cash-flow bond. The target carries a further 10.0% liquidity discount on top of a cost of equity that already includes a country premium and a levered beta of 2.05: that is a double discount, and we disclose it rather than bury it, because a 14.6% free float against the exchange's minimum is a real exit constraint [S0].

What would change our view? Four signposts, in order of importance. First, a sustained gross margin above 7.0% for two consecutive quarters, which would tell us the spread is structural and not cyclical [S3]. Second, working capital held below 53.0% of sales through a year of growth, which would prove the company can grow without consuming cash [S2]. Third, net debt below USD54.4m by the end of FY2027E, which would take the interest burden off the equity [S2][S3]. Fourth, and the one we would need before turning constructive at any price, evidence that the related-party purchase line is priced on arm's-length terms — a disclosure the annual report does not currently make [S2].

Latinusa is a controlled company in the fullest sense. Insiders hold 85.4% of the capital and the free float is 14.6% [S0]. That free float is below the exchange's minimum for a company of this market capitalisation: the registry (asof 27 October 2026) shows a float below the required level, tiered by market capitalisation, with the next step — reaching the minimum — dated 31 March 2029 [S0]. The remediation route is the one the exchange allows: a share issue or a sale by the controlling holders, not a delisting, so the disclosure is a dated constraint on any large buyer rather than an immediate event. It matters for the valuation twice: the exit pool is narrow, and any issue that dilutes the controlling block is the obvious way to fix it. The controlling shareholder sits inside the Nippon Steel group, and the same group supplies a material share of the company's raw materials through its trading arm: 29.3 USD m of purchases in FY2025, down from 49.1 USD m in FY2024 [S2]. That is the central governance fact about this equity. The party that controls the company also sits on the other side of its largest cost line, and the annual report gives the transaction amount but not the pricing mechanism or a benchmark against third-party quotes [S2]. We treat the relationship as disclosed and audited rather than improper — there is no finding, no qualification and no enforcement action — but a minority holder cannot independently verify the transfer price, and that caps the multiple the market should be willing to pay.

There is no evidence of the value-destruction channels that usually sit alongside control on this exchange. The share count has not changed since listing, so there has been no rights issue, no discounted private placement to an affiliate and no buyback [S2]. We found no pledged controlling stake in the filings, no special-monitoring-board status and no special notation on the listing [S2]. Related-party sales are not disclosed as a revenue channel; the gravity is all on the purchase side. Working capital is the one place where related-party exposure could hide, and the receivables book is not disclosed by counterparty [S2].

The board is small and the audit is done by a mid-tier firm rather than a Big Four practice [S2]. The audit opinion for the last fiscal year is unqualified, the financial statements are prepared under PSAK and presented in US dollars, and there has been no auditor change or restatement during the period we cover [S2]. We would flag two governance details as optics rather than manipulation: the dividend, at a payout of 30.0% of profit, sits at the floor of the stated policy and is small in absolute terms — a few rupiah a share — so it is not a signal of confidence either way [S2]; and the company's investor-relations page circulates analyst commentary, which we did not read, use or cite [S2]. The listing has existed since 2009 with a stable share count and no corporate action, which is a genuine positive in a market where per-share value leaks through serial issuance.

On ESG the exposure is industrial rather than reputational. Tinplate rolling is energy-intensive and the Cilegon site sits in an industrial zone with the air-quality and effluent obligations that implies; the company has invested in a once-through boiler and in the certifications that qualify it as a food-contact supplier, which are both a cost and a moat [S2]. Tin itself carries a conflict-minerals dimension that its food and beverage customers audit, and the fact that the tin is contracted from a domestic producer helps on traceability [S2]. Workforce is small at 214.0 people, with no disclosed labour dispute or safety incident of material size in the period [S2]. We score governance as the dominant ESG risk and the environmental dimension as manageable, with the caveat that a single-site operation carries concentration risk that no amount of certification removes.

The near-term calendar is dominated by evidence on the spread, not by corporate events. The full-year 2026 results, due early in 2027, will settle whether the nine-month improvement in gross profit survives a fourth quarter of higher tin and a seasonally weaker order book [S3]. The 2027 annual report will disclose whether the contracted tin volume — 595 t for 2026 — is being renewed at similar terms and whether the related-party purchase amount is falling as a share of cost [S3][S2]. Any trade-remedy decision affecting imported tinplate is a binary event for the spread and will move the stock more than the earnings print does [S2]. A dividend declaration at the low end of the payout range would be the default expectation; one above the policy range would be worth investigating for what it says about cash [S2].

Between formal catalysts we monitor four things, in this order: the gross margin quarter by quarter, since it is the whole thesis; the receivables balance, because it is the mechanism by which a good quarter becomes a bad balance sheet; the tin contract volume and the LME price it references; and the daily traded value, because at current liquidity a position cannot be exited on the numbers and the price is a flow variable rather than a valuation signal [S0][S2]. We do not monitor the share price as an input; we monitor it as an output and as a warning about the float.

The variant view, stated plainly for the record: the market is treating Latinusa as a cyclical recovery whose earnings will re-rate toward the boom multiple [S0]. We think the recovery is real and the re-rating is not, because the return on the plant is below the cost of capital even in a good year and the working capital structure turns growth into a cash drain. That is a SELL at Rp140 with a target of Rp18. The strongest argument against us is that trade protection plus a domestic monopoly gives the company pricing power we have not seen it exercise yet; if the next two quarters show margin holding above the top of its historical range, we will be wrong quickly and by a lot, and the signposts in the risk section are how we will know it.

bear.narrative: Import competition from China and Korea intensifies, the 2026 tin price is not passed through (tin +20% with half the cost recovered in price), the rupiah slips a further 5% against the dollar while the whole receivable book stays in rupiah, so the gross margin gives back the 2026 improvement; volume growth stalls at 3%. EBITDA then barely covers interest, the working-capital release that flatters a shrinking balance sheet is the only cash source, and the equity floors at its limited-liability value and no more.

bull.narrative: Trade-remedy enforcement and higher freight contain imports, the premium RTD and milk contracts lift mix as management plans (+11% sales volume), tin eases 20% below the 2026 squeeze toward the desk's USD37,000/t anchor and the rupiah firms, so the gross margin holds at the top of its historical range and the planned capacity is absorbed. The plant then earns a return closer to its replacement cost and a consolidating owner could justify paying above the Gordon-consistent book.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +15.8% holds the fourth quarter at the prior-year fourth quarter: the nine months to September 2026 printed USD116.8m (+23.2% y/y; 9M2025 USD94.8m) [S3], which leaves FY2025's Q4 of USD45.1m (FY2025 USD139.8m less 9M2025 USD94.8m) as the flat run-rate, i.e. a base year close to management's "about USD160m" target rather than below the actual run-rate [S2][S4]. Q3 2026 alone was stronger still, so this is the conservative end of the observable range, not a seasonal cut. FY2027E-FY2030E +4.0%/4.0%/4.0%/3.5% assume national tinplate demand recovering toward the 200kt level the company cites with no market-share gain, and USD selling prices flat in nominal terms after the 2023-2025 deflation [S4][S2]. Terminal 2.0% is below long-run USD nominal growth: a mature, import-competed converted-product business should not outgrow its end market forever.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 6.7% for FY2026E is the nine-month actual (gross profit USD7.8m on sales USD116.8m = 6.69%) [S3]. Management's USD3m net-profit guidance cannot be reached at this margin: on the nine-month cost base it would need a gross margin well above anything the company has printed in the last five years (the best year, FY2022, was 7.7%), so the base case keeps the observed margin and does not adopt guidance that the company itself missed by 9% of its sales target in FY2025 [S2][S3][S4]. 6.9%-7.0% thereafter reflects a modest mix shift to premium/RTD and milk can stock (milk share of sales rose from 25.51% to 27.59%) plus the tin price normalising from the 2026 squeeze back to the desk's USD37,000/t through-cycle anchor, net of the rupiah earnings channel: revenue is rupiah while steel and tin are imported in dollars, so a weaker rupiah is a margin cost, not a translation [S2][S3].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Gross SG&A is the nine-month run rate (administrative USD2.07m + selling and distribution USD2.09m on sales USD116.8m = 3.56%) [S3], and management is holding it flat in dollars while revenue grows, so the gross ratio drifts from 3.5% to 3.2% on a fixed-cost base of c.USD5.5m [S4]. This line is carried net of recurring scrap sales, because the LK puts sales of scrap inside operating profit and the historical line here (gross profit less EBIT) is already on that basis: scrap was USD970,461 in FY2025 (0.69% of sales) and USD677,093 in the nine months to September 2026 (0.58%) [S2][S3], sales that recur every year because they are the trimmed offcut of the same 160kt rolling programme, not a one-off asset disposal. FY2026E therefore takes 0.6pp off the gross ratio and 0.6pp off each later year — the lower of the two observed rates, so the credit is not overstated [S2][S3].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: property depreciation charged to all functions was USD1.82m in FY2025 (F6, note 9) plus right-of-use depreciation of USD0.09m (F8, note 18), i.e. 1.37% of sales, against the 0.18% the data pack carries — the pack understates the charge roughly eightfold [S2]. We hold 1.45% forward, a little above the restated ratio, because the revamp and boiler capex commissioned in 2026 adds a full year of depreciation on the new assets.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash-flow capex was USD0.78m in FY2025 (0.56% of sales) and USD0.76m in FY2024 [S2] — below the restated depreciation charge, i.e. the plant has been harvested. The base case lifts capex to 1.3% (c.USD2.1m) because the once-through boiler, conductor-roll and revamp items the AR describes must be sustained to hold 160,000 t of capacity and the food-safety/green-industry certifications [S2]; it stays below D&A, so the asset base slowly shrinks in real terms.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was USD77.4m on sales of USD139.8m in FY2025 (55%) and USD81.7m on USD155.7m in FY2024 (52.5%), a two-year average of 53% [S2], and it was USD81.3m at 30 September 2026 (trade receivables USD61.95m plus inventories USD29.80m less trade payables USD10.49m) on an annualised revenue run-rate of about USD155.7m — 52% [S3]. Receivables run near 145 days and payables about 25 days because the substrate is imported while sales are rupiah, so half of revenue is structurally tied up. 53% is therefore the sourced through-cycle ratio and is applied to every year; the earlier 46% was the 30 June seasonal trough and is discarded [S2][S3][S4].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective tax was 31.5% of pre-tax profit (USD0.45m on USD1.42m) and the nine-month 2026 charge 24.0% (USD0.49m on USD2.03m); 25% sits between the two and just above the 22% statutory rate, allowing for non-deductible items [S2][S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The P&L charge is the contracted legacy rate: FY2025 interest expense of USD2.43m on opening debt of USD63.3m is 3.8% and the nine-month 2026 finance cost of USD1.93m on opening debt of USD54.3m annualises to 4.7% [S2][S3]. 4.7% is used for the P&L because it is the latest observed rate over a full nine months. The WACC uses a different, forward marginal cost of debt (risk-free plus the corporate spread, 6.87%) because new debt raised to fund working capital will not be priced at the legacy contracted rate; the gap between the two is disclosed in section 4 rather than smoothed away, and it is a WACC input, never a P&L input.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was USD0.095m on opening cash of USD8.44m in FY2025 (1.1%), with USD0.12m of finance income in the nine months to September 2026 [S2][S3]; 1.0% holds the deposit yield.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt did not fall in 2026: short-term bank loans were USD53.87m at 31 December 2025 (total debt including leases USD54.33m) and USD58.87m at 30 September 2026, because the 23.2% revenue recovery was funded by a working-capital build (receivables to USD61.95m, inventories to USD29.80m) [S2][S3]. The base case therefore continues to fund working capital with debt: +USD4.9m in FY2026E (the observed nine-month move), +USD3.0m in FY2027E and +USD2.0m in FY2028E as revenue grows at 4% with a 53% working-capital ratio, then zero in FY2029E and a first repayment of USD2.0m in FY2030E. The earlier repayment path was inconsistent with both the LK and a growing working-capital ratio [S3].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items (incl. net FX)
assumptions.basis: The FX line is the inverted currency exposure. Net loss on currency exchange was USD0.80m in the nine months to September 2026 (USD0.37m a year earlier), driven by the rupiah-denominated liabilities (77.5% of short-term bank loans, IDR 821.5bn) against dollar funding [S3]. FY2026E carries the FX loss grossed to four quarters (USD1.07m) net of other income at the nine-month run rate (USD309,874, i.e. USD0.41m a year) [S3]. FY2027E-FY2030E carry USD0.78m of annual translation loss on the IDR 821.5bn of rupiah debt, less the same USD0.41m of other income, which is recurring: it was USD722,044 in FY2025 and USD792,442 in FY2024, and USD309,874 in the nine months to September 2026 [S2][S3]. Other income is not an operating line in the data pack — it sits below EBIT in the LK — so it is credited here rather than in the operating margin, while sales of scrap, which the LK does put inside operating profit, are netted in opex_pct [S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interest on the balance sheet at any date in the data pack or the LK [S2].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Stated policy is to pay out 30%-40% of net profit each year, subject to cash and GMS approval; the FY2025 dividend actually paid in April 2026 equates to 30% of that year's net profit, so 30% is the observed floor of the policy rather than an assumption of generosity [S2].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 2,523.35m shares issued and fully paid, unchanged since the 2009 IPO; no rights issue or buyback announced [S2].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.0% nominal in USD — the house default and at or below long-run US inflation, well below Indonesian nominal GDP. Indonesian tinplate demand has fallen from a 250kt peak in 2022 to c.200kt, so the terminal rate is not a growth bet: it prices a mature, import-competed market growing with the canning customers' own volumes [S2][S4].

challenges.challenge: The bridge and opening working capital are 30 June 2026, but the 30 September LK is in the packet: S3 p.4 shows cash 8,476,144 and short-term bank loans 58,871,391, i.e. net debt about USD50.4m before leases against the USD35.7m in model.valuation and in the report; the tax-refund claim is 7,173,726, not the 5,201,869 [F29] in the bridge; trade receivables 61,954,479 plus inventories 29,801,615 less payables 9,550,670 + 934,800 give operating NWC near USD81.5m against the 65.3m June figure the forecast starts from. On the September balance sheet the base equity value of USD4.65m is negative before the tax claim, and each USD1m of net debt is about Rp7/share. The report's 'receivables fell by a fifth from the year-end balance' (fund record:265) is contradicted by S3 p.4: 61,954,479 vs 60,789,885 at December, up 1.9%.
challenges.answer: Rolled the valuation to the 30 September 2026 balance sheet from S3 as bs_cash/bs_debt/bs_equity facts: net debt USD50.4m not USD35.7m, tax claim USD7.174m (F33) not USD5.202m, and working capital USD81.3m. Target moves from 58 to 11 because the DCF equity value is now negative before the claim.

challenges.challenge: The currency exposure is inverted. S3 note 6 shows all trade receivables in rupiah ('Rupiah 61,977,422'); S3 note 27 shows IDR 821,457,201,611 of short-term bank loans = USD45,641,582 of USD58,871,391, i.e. 77.5%; S4 quotes management 'seluruh bahan baku diimpor sementara penjualan wajib rupiah' (all raw materials imported while sales must be rupiah). fund record:121-122 nevertheless says 'output is sold in dollars, the P&L is hedged at the gross-margin line' and fund record:397 says 'Its debt is dollar-denominated and floating in part'. fund record:15 applies 'no FX translation' and other_nonop is zero, so the USD800,250 FX loss actually booked in 9M2026 (S3) vanishes from every forecast year.
challenges.answer: Currency exposure corrected everywhere: revenue and all receivables are rupiah (F37), inputs are imported dollars, 77.5% of bank loans are rupiah (F38), and an FX loss line now runs through other_nonop from the 9M2026 actual (F36). Both inverted sentences in the report are rewritten, and the assumptions FX basis is fixed.

challenges.challenge: The stated basis of the SELL is false on the report's own numbers. fund record:354-356 says 'Across defensible ranges of the working capital ratio, capex intensity and terminal growth the equity value stays in the tens of rupiah per share and never reaches the current price', yet model.sensitivities grid 2 puts the 12-month value at 168.98 with revenue growth at 2% and base margin, and 178.92 at base growth with gross margin +1pp - both above Rp140 - and the grid spans 0 to 526. The grid's axes are revenue growth and gross margin, not the working-capital/capex/terminal-growth axes the prose describes. fund record:362 then renders 'What does the price imply? 0.0' and claims Rp140 needs 2022-peak margins, while model.reverse_dcf solves the same price to a revenue-growth add of -0.018848, i.e. 2.1% growth at base margins, below the 4.0% base.
challenges.answer: The robustness paragraph is rewritten to the grid actually published, including the growth axis where a slower path is worth more, and it now explains why: at 53% working capital the incremental return is far below WACC, so the base follows the company plan rather than the value-maximising path, and the WACC/terminal-growth axis is the one the target rests on.

challenges.challenge: The cost of capital is internally inconsistent and circular. model.valuation.coc uses kd_pre_tax 6.872% (rf 4.872% + the macro deck's 2.0pp corporate spread), but the same model charges interest at assumptions.cost_of_debt 4.5% (interest_expense 2.44m on 54.33m of opening debt), and the filings show 3.8% in FY2025 and 4.7% annualised in 9M2026 [S2][S3] - the report never explains why the same debt costs 4.5% in the P&L and 6.87% in the WACC. The 2.0x D/E used to relever beta to 2.048 and set the equity weight at one third is the market capitalisation ratio, but at the model's own equity value of USD4.65m net debt is 7.7x equity and at the target it is 4.4x, so the WACC is computed on a capital structure the target contradicts. WACC also uses a 22% tax rate against 25% in the P&L.
challenges.answer: One P&L cost of debt at 4.7% (the 9M2026 annualised actual) replaces 4.5%; the WACC's 6.87% forward marginal rate is now disclosed and explained rather than left inconsistent, and the 2.0x relevering is shown to be below the market's own three times, so the circularity is disclosed in the direction that favours the stock.

challenges.challenge: Working capital is set at 46% of revenue in every year while fund record:115-118 states FY2025 was 55%, FY2024 52.5% and '53% is the two-year average', and then uses 46% anyway. 46% is the 30 June 2026 balance (datapack nwc 65.285 on an annualised Q2 revenue run-rate), a seasonal trough, not the through-cycle ratio. This is unjustified optimism on the single lever the report calls knife-edged: each 1pp of NWC/revenue is worth about a tenth of equity value, so 7pp of understatement inflates the target materially. fund record:253 also prints 'USD77.4m, or 46.0% of revenue' when 77.4/139.8 is 55.4%.
challenges.answer: Working capital set at 53% of revenue in every year, the sourced two-year average, with the 46% trough discarded; the 46.0% arithmetic sentence is gone and the forecast debt path now funds the 53% ratio, which lowers the target materially.

challenges.challenge: Two-thirds of the enterprise value (67.8%) is terminal value, and the implied exit is 3.6x FY2030E EBITDA (model tv 35.06 / ebitda FY2030E 9.70). The report never states, sources or tests that multiple, while it does compute an 8.2x forward EV/EBITDA [S0] and dismisses it as boom-era - a 3.6x perpetual exit is a far more aggressive judgement than the 8.2x it rejects. At a 5x exit the terminal value alone adds about USD9.6m of present value, roughly Rp68/share. The house card's multiple-survival test and the reinvestment/ROIIC output are missing.
challenges.answer: The implied exit is now stated explicitly from the published terminal value and FY2030E EBITDA, tested against the 8.2x forward and the last actual year's multiple, and justified by the fact that terminal FCFF is struck after the full working-capital and capex charge. The report also shows what a five times exit would add.

challenges.challenge: The valuation assigns no value to the asset base or to control. Equity book is USD56.6m with a USD11.6m revaluation surplus [S2 p.115] against a market capitalisation of USD19.6m; the plant is 160kt of installed capacity and the sole domestic producer [S2 p.28/73/174]; 55% of the register sits with the NSC/Mitsui/NSTC/Metal One consortium, with Krakatau Steel at 20.1% and ASABRI at 10.3% [S2 p.6/10/24]. The bull case is +/-1pp revenue growth and +/-1.5pp margin, with no strategic, liquidation or replacement-value floor and no statement of what a consolidating owner would pay.
challenges.answer: Added an asset and control-value cross-check: book equity of USD58.1m including the USD11.6m revaluation surplus (F32, F39), the strategic register, and 160,000t of sole-producer capacity (F11), with the explicit reason the holder does nothing — no sale process, a below-minimum float, and a going concern funded by state-linked banks.

challenges.challenge: Volume is a 'qualitative overlay' (fund record:11) rather than a modelled line, so the operating leverage of the recovery never reaches the bull case. The company has 160kt of capacity [S2 p.28] against national demand of 200kt (peak 250kt) [S4], plans +12% production/+11% sales for FY2026, and 9M2026 revenue is already +23.2% (S3 116,775,903), with sheet sales up about 39%. flags.justification: The expected return follows from three sourced drivers, recomputed on the engine's current numbers. First, the spread: gross margin was 5.8% in FY2025 and 6.69% in the nine months to September 2026, and EBIT of USD3.8m in FY2025 and USD4.33m in 9M2026 (gross profit USD7.81m less unallocated opex USD4.16m plus the USD0.68m scrap credit) does not cover an 18.6% cost of equity on USD58.1m of book equity, an ROE of under 4% [S2][S3 p.81]. Second, working capital at 53% of sales consumes the recovery: nine-month revenue rose 23.2% while receivables reached USD61.95m and inventories USD29.80m, funded by USD58.87m of bank loans at 30 September 2026, so free cash flow to the firm was negative in the first nine months and growth at a 4% ROIIC destroys value against a 9.76% WACC [S3]. Third, the balance sheet: enterprise value of USD34.4m against net debt of USD50.4m (bank loans USD58.87m less cash USD8.48m) leaves the DCF equity value at minus USD8.78m before the USD7.17m tax claim, so the base case floors at zero and the target is carried by the bull branch. The reverse DCF solves today's Rp140 to FY2027E revenue growth of 0.76%, below our 4.0% base rather than above it: the market is pricing a path more than three points slower than the plan because slower growth consumes less working capital, and even that path is worth only the share price, not the asset or control value [S0][S2][S3].
